title: Game development and game design

noc.title: Software developers and programmers
noc.applies_when: The home code. "Computer game developer" and "interactive media developer" are named examples. Any gameplay, engine, tools or systems programming seat.

noc.title: Software engineers and designers
noc.applies_when: Engine and architecture-level seats. Steinbach RCIP code.

noc.title: Graphic designers and illustrators
noc.applies_when: Only where the seat is genuinely art-led rather than technical. Weaker, and not where he should aim.

adjacent: technical artist. Simulation and real-time 3D outside games is the underrated half of this lane and it is where the Haply Robotics haptics work lands perfectly: training simulation
industrial digital twins and visualisation all hire exactly this skill set and compete for far fewer candidates than games studios do

skills.evidence: Custom game engine built from scratch in C++ and OpenGL. Haply Robotics C++ work bridging CHAI 3D.

skills.name: C#
skills.evidence: Haply Robotics: Unity scripts, native plugins, and C# to C++ interop for real-time bidirectional haptics.

skills.name: A named engine
skills.asked_for: Unreal or Unity. Postings name one, rarely both
skills.evidence: Both. Unity through Haply Robotics and coursework; Unreal Engine 5 through Death Bridge and the JKR channel work.

skills.name: Gameplay programming
skills.evidence: Death Bridge implementation plus the Fanshawe programme.

skills.name: 3D maths
skills.evidence: Custom engine: rendering pipeline, animation, physics basics, collision detection, all hand-built.

skills.name: Version control
skills.asked_for: Git, and awareness that games teams often use Perforce
skills.evidence: Maintained public repos. Perforce specifically is a gap, see Important.

skills.name: Debugging and profiling
skills.asked_for: Finding the bug and finding the frame cost
skills.evidence: Real debugging across engine and interop work. Formal profiling against a frame budget is not evidenced.
skills.limit: Formal profiling against a frame budget is not evidenced.

skills.name: Game design fundamentals
skills.asked_for: Loops, pacing, player feedback, why a mechanic works
skills.evidence: Death Bridge is his own design work, so the thinking is real. It has not been tested against players or a design review.
skills.limit: It has not been tested against players or a design review.

skills.evidence: Custom shaders and a hand-built OpenGL rendering pipeline. Genuinely uncommon at junior level.

skills.name: Perforce
skills.asked_for: The standard version control in games studios
skills.note: Named often. Cheap to close and worth doing.

skills.asked_for: Something someone else can actually play
skills.evidence: Death Bridge is in progress. This is the single highest-leverage gap in the lane.
skills.limit: This is the single highest-leverage gap in the lane.

skills.evidence: Death Bridge environments. Not evidenced as a standalone discipline.
skills.limit: Not evidenced as a standalone discipline.

skills.evidence: UI work across engine and app projects.
skills.limit: UI work across engine and app projects.

skills.evidence: Custom engine covers both; Haply work is multi-physics environments.

positioning:
This lane is stronger than it looks on a resume summary. A junior applicant who has built a game engine from scratch in C++ and OpenGL with shaders, a rendering pipeline, animation, physics and collision is not a typical junior applicant, and neither is one who wrote C# to C++ interop for real-time haptics on a research project. Lead with the engine and the Haply work, in that order, because they demonstrate the thing studios actually screen for at junior level: can this person reason about systems and performance, or have they only followed tutorials.

The honest gap is the one every self-taught and recently-graduated game candidate has: no finished, playable thing that someone else has played. Death Bridge is in progress and a playable vertical slice would move this lane more than any additional skill. A game jam would do the same job faster and adds the team-working evidence he is missing everywhere.

Most postings in this lane grade Tier B on current statuses, moving to Tier A once there is a playable build. Perforce is the one cheap named gap.
interview_watch: Expect a technical screen on C++ or C# fundamentals and 3D maths, and expect questions about the engine project specifically since it is the most interesting thing on the resume. Be ready to explain a design decision inside it and what you would do differently. Expect "what games do you play and what would you change about one" for design-leaning seats, which rewards a specific mechanical answer over enthusiasm. For simulation and real-time roles, lead with Haply rather than Death Bridge.
not_required: Published shipped titles, AAA credits, or a games-specific degree beyond what he has. A posting hard-requiring shipped commercial titles has effectively failed the seniority gate.

notes.heading: Intro
notes.text:
New in v3.5. NOC 21232, TEER 1. Read 00-index.md for the Status conventions and tier rules.

The headline finding. NOC 21232 Software developers and programmers is TEER 1, and its illustrative example titles include "computer game developer", "interactive media developer" and "multimedia developer". Game development is not a weaker code than software development. It is the same code. That means this lane carries the full PR value of lane 4: North Bay RCIP lists 21232, MPNP listed it as of v3.1 (re-verify), AIP covers it from a designated Atlantic employer, and Ontario's Workforce Priority stream takes it with a qualifying offer. This lane costs him nothing on the immigration side, which was the thing worth checking before building it.

notes.heading: Credentials
notes.text: - Game Development: Advanced Programming, Fanshawe College, London ON (2023 to 2024). A named game development credential, which is what most junior game postings ask for and most junior applicants substitute a portfolio for. He has both. - Master of Computer Applications, Anna University (2020 to 2022). Carries the post-secondary credential requirement for the Ontario Workforce Priority stream.

notes.heading: Sourcing notes
notes.text: Geography reality: the Canadian games market concentrates in Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver and Quebec City, with a real cluster in Kitchener-Waterloo that is commutable-adjacent from London. Montreal and Quebec City postings frequently require French, which is a language-gate drop, so expect Quebec yield to be low and do not read that as the lane being dry.
